segment.text: 滝は、あまり創作（小説）のことばかり想つてゐるのが重苦しくなつたのでスケツチ箱をさげて散歩に出かけた。――石段を降つて、又ひよろ〳〵と降つて行く海辺へ近い松林の中途であつた。彼は、風景よりも人通りを気にして小径を出はずれると頭につかえる松の矮林の中へ腰をかゞめて姿を没した。そして、丘の切れ端に来て月見草の間に胡坐をした。遥かの距離だが、灰色に光つてゐる砂地に風にもてあそばれてゐる風呂敷のやうなものが四つも五つも切りに堂々廻りをしてゐるので、何だらうと思つて見あげると低く大輪を描いて舞つてゐる鴎達の影であつた。

sentences.text: 滝は、あまり創作（小説）のことばかり想つてゐるのが重苦しくなつたのでスケツチ箱をさげて散歩に出かけた。
――石段を降つて、又ひよろ〳〵と降つて行く海辺へ近い松林の中途であつた。
彼は、風景よりも人通りを気にして小径を出はずれると頭につかえる松の矮林の中へ腰をかゞめて姿を没した。
そして、丘の切れ端に来て月見草の間に胡坐をした。
遥かの距離だが、灰色に光つてゐる砂地に風にもてあそばれてゐる風呂敷のやうなものが四つも五つも切りに堂々廻りをしてゐるので、何だらうと思つて見あげると低く大輪を描いて舞つてゐる鴎達の影であつた。

segment.text: 暑い二日日の夕方、遠見の海のスケツチ板を仕上げて、だが滝は、たゞボーツとしてぶらぶら帰つて来ると石段の下あたりで彼の行衛を探してゞもゐたらしくうろうろしてゐる細君に出遇つた。

segment.text: 「半分位ひ――」と彼は何の顧慮もなさげに云ひ放つた。――彼は、この頃全くの架空的な物語の構想に没頭してゐた。ペンを執りさへすれば半分も何もない何時からでも一気呵勢に書き綴れると思つてゐた。いや、書くことなどは懸念もしなかつた。どうかするとあまりに放縦な想ひに眩惑されて重苦しくなることさへあつたが、ペンを執つて散文化してしまふことが、丁度他人と言葉を交へる時と同じやうに稚拙な文章が廻りくどかつたりして折角の感興にそぐはなかつた。

segment.text: 滝は他人の言葉が気になつたのは近頃珍らしかつた。――彼は、何といふこともなしに歪んだ神経に目醒めたかのやうに、不快な寒さに襲はれてしまつた。己れの眼が、明るみにある梟の眼である！　そんな自嘲に陥つた。茫漠たる想ひにばかり酔つてゐる己れの存在が周囲の者の内心に如何な悲しみを与へてゐることだらう――そんな弱々しく尤もらしい屈托などにまで走つた。また、これまで自分が書いて来た現実風の小説も、そして己れが実に浮々と愚かな態度でこの世に処して来たこと――それらが悉く拙劣な間違ひだらけな「雪景色」になつて、すると忽ち怖ろしい吹雪が起り、彼は目を瞑ぢ胸を伏せて、一散に白皚々の曠野に逃げ出さなければ居られなかつた、何にも見えない……。

segment.text: そして彼は、うと〳〵としながら容易に自分の部屋へ引き取らうとはしなかつた。滝が書斎に定めてゐる部屋には、どうしたわけか電灯が引いてなかつた。増築が出来かゝつた儘で四五年来も投げ放しになつてゐたのだが、察するところ其処は仏間にでもする思案があつたらしかつた。彼は永い間の昼夜の転換を取り戻すために、反つてそれを幸ひにして直ぐに引き込めるであらう電灯を其処だけは点さなかつた。そして昼間だけを、慣れないので極く稀であつたが海へも行かれない曇り日などに机に向つてゐた。夜にかゝる場合があると、半ば物数奇から行灯や燭台の光りを頼りにして読書をしたり、それこそ真に愚かな「雪景色」のやうな物思ひに耽つたりした。

segment.text: 彼女は、物哀しさの甘さが厭に露骨で、懸声に似たコーラスの個所がワザとらしいといふ理由で、そしてアメリカ水夫の歌なんて古く俗つぽいといふ反趣味とで、滝が吾知らず口笛で吹いてゐるのをきいても鼻についたと称して耳をふさぐのであつた。帆綱を巻きあげ、舵を執り、マストに駆け昇る――そんな事実の行動に伴うて、伴奏される歌調が、力を惜まずロープを巻きあげる腕に合せて思はず叫ぶ「コーラス」が、安逸の素面から口吟まれゝば厭に露骨でワザとらしく見えるのも当然だが――大洋の真ツたゞ中で立ち働く者の胸のうち……そんなものは、都で生れ都でのみ育つた不良少女あがりの細君には夢にも想像し得ないに違ひない。

segment.text: 泥棒の忍び声のやうな囁きで滝は、目を醒すと一処に床を蹴つた。細君から電話が掛つて来る時分には彼は、酒徳利の載つた朝飯の膳を縁側近くに用意して、新しく取り寄せた箱根細工の脇側などに凭りかゝりながら深刻な眼つきでＡ・Ｂの活躍を視守つた。――滝は、「頭の中へ持ち応えてゐる六ヶ敷い仕事！」も「愉快な韻文的空想！」も「架空の物語！」も「眼の前の細事は一切没却した広大無辺な無呵有の空に咽んでゐた筈の忘我の詩境！」も「ナンシー・リー」も「電話！」も「怖ろしい吹雪！」も「たゞ見る一面の雪景色！」も「……一気呵勢！」も、何も彼も鵞毛の如く散乱して、ひたすら池を瞶め、獲物を待つ尊大なブルジヨアであつた。

sentences.text: 泥棒の忍び声のやうな囁きで滝は、目を醒すと一処に床を蹴つた。
細君から電話が掛つて来る時分には彼は、酒徳利の載つた朝飯の膳を縁側近くに用意して、新しく取り寄せた箱根細工の脇側などに凭りかゝりながら深刻な眼つきでＡ・Ｂの活躍を視守つた。
――滝は、「頭の中へ持ち応えてゐる六ヶ敷い仕事！」
も「愉快な韻文的空想！」
も「架空の物語！」
も「眼の前の細事は一切没却した広大無辺な無呵有の空に咽んでゐた筈の忘我の詩境！」
も「ナンシー・リー」も「電話！」
も「怖ろしい吹雪！」
も「たゞ見る一面の雪景色！」
も「……一気呵勢！」
も、何も彼も鵞毛の如く散乱して、ひたすら池を瞶め、獲物を待つ尊大なブルジヨアであつた。

segment.text: 池のまはりは、火事場のやうな騒ぎであつた。年寄りを初め、自動車屋の集金人、料理屋の掛け取り、女郎屋の「馬」、レストランの亭主、酒屋の番頭、待合の「お帳場」――それ等の人々が、各々双肌脱ぎになつてＡの指揮にもとづきながら懸声そろへてポンプのハンドルをあをつてゐた。無駄口一つ叩く者がなく一同は息を切つて眼前の仕事に没頭してゐた。上げては降し、降しては上げる満身の力と共に思はずほとばしる彼等の懸声には恰もナンシー・リーのコーラスのやうな底力が籠り、颯爽の気に満ちてゐた。

chapter_summaries.0: Part One. Taki, oppressed by thinking about fiction, walks with sketch-box to the pines above the sea. That evening his wife, who lives separately, meets him by the stone steps hunting for him. They circle through the carp in the pointless pond, the house soon to be cleared for a warehouse, his lack of sentiment, his stalled架空 story he could write 'in one burst', a future trip and Tokyo lodging. Two tattooed tobishoku fail to catch the carp in reddening water. Indoors the wife mistakes his finished summer seascape for a snowscape in midsummer; he flushes, falls into a blizzard hallucination of guilt and flight, then covers with sheepish talk of evening loneliness and heat.

hard_spots.why_hard: A and B speak fast, elided working-class coastal speech with obscenity at the edges; narrator even glosses 手前え as first-person. Must sound rougher and funnier than Taki without English eye-dialect caricature or pinning them to another country. Keep speaker attribution floating where Japanese leaves it floating.

Paired tattoos — A's finished dragon and clouds vs B's abandoned hannya outline — plus Taki's unasked question about why B stopped. Do not explain or complete; the unfinished tattoo belongs with the unfinished house, book, carp-catch and trip.

The snowscape detonation (owl's eyes in daylight, peony-petal sinful snow) is meant to be a little too much, then punctured flat. p160 lists Taki's slogans back verbatim as they scatter like goose down. Keep images literal and slightly overripe; keep the catalogue recognisable as quotation, not paraphrase.

Harmonica set (Ai Ai Ai, Valencia, Light Cavalry, Tokyo March, American Patrol, Nancy Lee, Mori no Kajiya) was modern popular music in 1927. Nancy Lee travels from father's whaling tale to Taki's whistling to wife's disgust to creditors' pump chorus. Keep title untranslated, unexplained in text; let wife's 'old and vulgar American sailors' song' stand against Taki's sentimentality without adjudicating. Father's tale keeps hearsay colouring ('he used to say').

Restaurant haggling over money and drinking leaves speakers to inference with gaps (…………) and fragments. Do not assign names the Japanese withholds; keep stichomythic brevity and the flat ten-yen reveal.

Slow caretaker patter on the pine road is cut by Taki's parenthesised lightning thoughts (telephone! it's mine! sell it!). Keep them typographically and rhythmically separate — drunk insight inside a slow scene — and keep final staggering simile (like walking in deep snow) literal as callback to snowscape.

Taki slides from eavesdropper to imitator of A's cadence to shouting general/impresario (nets! beat them to death!). Must sound like a different man from the snowscape reverie, brutal and comic, not a polished narrator summarising.

motifs.english: Keep one fixed English — 'in one burst!' — wherever the slogan appears, from unwritten masterpiece to pumping the pond. The migration is the joke and the verdict.
motifs.why: Taki's motto, excuse and sedative: having thought it he can relax into dream. Finally attaches to the only decisive act, performed by others draining the pond.

motifs.english: Keep one plain verb — 'catch' — throughout; do not vary into grab/land/net. Let it toll from wife to workmen to Taki's bellowing.
motifs.why: The story's engine of frustration; pond clouds whenever anyone moves. Repetition in same words makes the mechanism audible.

motifs.english: Keep 'snowscape' as a hard noun everywhere, never softened to snowy scene/wintry view. Keep title Snowscape.
motifs.why: Wife's mild remark that the finished summer seascape looks like a snowscape triggers full blizzard hallucination and becomes indictment of his fiction and life; recurs in catalogue and final staggering simile.

motifs.english: Do not translate; keep 'Nancy Lee' romanised and unexplained in text. Gloss only in margin if needed.
motifs.why: Travels from father's deck-song to Taki's whistling habit to wife's ostentatious ear-covering to creditors' pump chorus — the one genuine collective vigour, owned by men he owes.

motifs.english: Keep 'telephone' literal and abrupt wherever it erupts; keep exclamatory repetition in drunk scene.
motifs.why: Sudden saleable asset and excuse for absence; daily morning call he dreads; his Hang up! in p164 is his only decisive gesture.

motifs.english: Keep 'hold (it) in my head' fixed; keep 'the difficult work' fixed. They must read as self-quotation when listed back in p160.
motifs.motif: holding the work in the head / dream / fiction-talk
motifs.why: What stays unwritten while pond business fills the days; p160 throws his phrases back as goose down scattering at the sight of prey and money.

motifs.english: Keep cloud/mud vocabulary stable — cloudy, muddy, muddy water — not varied into turbid/murky by turns.
motifs.why: Physical correlative of the whole plot: every attempt to catch makes seeing impossible; clearing takes days. Deadpan mechanism, not metaphor to be polished.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for narrated action, preserving Japanese aspect shifts where they mark tableau vs event (e.g. frozen noon scene p180-181 in a still present-like past; ongoing states with 'would' avoided). Do not archaize to match historical kana.
narration.frame: Four numbered sections (一二三四) with diamond breaks; linear summer sequence over a few days (sketch walk → evening carp talk → bus-miss walk to town → drunken return → carp valuation and brothel → full-day hunt → pump-draining). Interior parenthetical flashes (telephone! sell it!) interrupt without leaving third person. Ends flatly on reported absence.
narration.narrator: Third-person, close to Taki but even-handed; never calls him lazy or absurd outright. Records dialogue, dialect and interior weather in the same level voice; pauses for relished description (tattoos, noon tableau, pump chorus) then collapses back to mud and bills.
narration.tense_habits: Literary Taishō-Shōwa written style mixing -ta past, -teiru progressive/resultative, and timeless description; dialogue in period colloquial; tense shifts mid-paragraph for tableau effect. Subjects and speakers routinely dropped.
timeline: I (p1-p70): hot second-day evening walk and sketch; wife meets Taki at stone steps; long talk on carp, doomed house, trip and Tokyo lodging; workmen fail; snowscape remark detonates reverie; dusk grappling in pond

II (p71-p146): same day to nightfall failure and drinking; moonlit pine-road walk with harmonica medley and Nancy Lee history; restaurant money haggling; drunken lantern walk home with telephone-selling inspiration
III (p147-p202): next days: 400-yen valuation via goldfish dealer, brothel night, day-long pond siege as Taki bellows and grandstands, evening admission of delay and Pin-ko arithmetic
IV (p203-p212): night insects and creditors gather; decision to pump pond dry in one burst; mass pumping to Nancy Lee-like chorus while Taki absent in Tokyo to buy a lamp

part_summaries.summary: Part One. Taki, oppressed by thinking about fiction, walks with sketch-box to the pines above the sea. That evening his wife, who lives separately, meets him by the stone steps hunting for him. They circle through the carp in the pointless pond, the house soon to be cleared for a warehouse, his lack of sentiment, his stalled架空 story he could write 'in one burst', a future trip and Tokyo lodging. Two tattooed tobishoku fail to catch the carp in reddening water. Indoors the wife mistakes his finished summer seascape for a snowscape in midsummer; he flushes, falls into a blizzard hallucination of guilt and flight, then covers with sheepish talk of evening loneliness and heat.

Part Two. The workmen fail again till dusk, then drink with the old caretaker couple and refuse to go home. Taki lies in the empty sitting room dreaming and postponing work; his unlit study (meant perhaps for an altar room) lets him keep day-night reversed. He and his wife walk the moonlit pine road missing the bus, discuss seasons, hear her harmonica (Ai Ai Ai, Valencia, Light Cavalry, Tokyo March, American Patrol) and quarrel lightly over Nancy Lee — his dead father's whaling song and his whistling habit she finds vulgar. In town he drinks too much despite promising not to; they haggle over ten yen; she leaves alone. Drunk and singing home, met by the lantern-bearing old man sent by his wife's telephone call, he has parenthetical flashes: the telephone is his! sell it! sell it tomorrow! — to protect head-work and travel — while staggering as if in deep snow.

Part Three. A reports the visiting goldfish dealer's valuation: about 400 yen if caught and handed over. Taki says 'Sell.' That night he takes A and B by car to the seaside brothel; drums sound. Next day the house bustles. A and B, with bounties, hunt all day while Taki watches from the veranda over breakfast and new Hakone woodwork, telephones his wife to stay away, and turns general-impresario: imitating A's speech, shouting nets!, beating the table, inviting hedge-peepers to best seats, ordering wading and killing. The noon tableau freezes (A leaning on a net-pole, B with cast-net, bubble bursting) then bursts again. By evening no catch; Taki counsels gentler methods, declares all will be sold, worries about face, and brags that the barmaid Pin-ko likes him, calculating brothel funds from the carp.

Part Four. Night frogs and insects; new creditors visit the orange-tree house. A and B resolve to borrow a hand-pump from a villa and drain the pond 'in one burst'. Taki watches the old man's abacus; travel waits on head-work; cloudy midsummer days, rumour of waves. Creditors of every trade — car shop collector, restaurant and brothel dunners, bar owner, liquor clerk, assignation-house clerk — strip and pump in unison to A's lead with Nancy Lee-chorus force, muddy water arcing to the roof. Taki is absent: gone to Tokyo, the caretaker says, to buy a lamp.

body.say: Passage wins over this bible where they conflict; record openness (speakers, mother, father's tale, sketch) as openness, not tidiness.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse. Note only what sentence cannot give: song titles, 400 yen / 10 yen scale, Buddhist altar-room extension, tattoo subjects (dragon, hannya), month-end payment custom, hand-pump and cast-net fishing. Never note what context supplies or resolve deliberate gaps.
style_sheet.author_voice: Makino's even, deadpan lyricism: capable of reportorial calm and sudden inflated reverie, then flat puncture. Protect comic disproportion — carp-hunt as battle, chorus, theatre — without winking. Keep grand phrases slightly too much (peony-petal snow, goose down, owl's eyes) so their collapse is funny then briefly sad. Same English must inflate and collapse.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Surname order; Taki for 滝 throughout (never 'Mr Taki' in narration). Keep Sensei only if text ever used it — it does not. Keep wife as 'my wife / his wife' or 'the wife' matching 細君, never invent a given name. Keep A and B as A and B. Keep Pin-ko hyphenated. Address forms (あなた, あんた, お爺さん, 奥さん, お母さん) rendered in plain English equivalents (you, old man/grandad, madam/wife, mother) with margin note on first use where needed.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Nancy Lee (ナンシー・リー) stays romanised in text. No other Japanese words retained in English text except as needed for nuance in margin (e.g. 一気呵勢, 細君). Food, clothing, housing terms translated; money in yen with figures kept exact.
style_sheet.quotation: Use double quotes for speech, single for thought-quotation and Taki's quoted-back slogans in p160. Keep parenthetical drunk flashes — (so there is a telephone!) etc. — in parentheses on their own lines/beats, rhythmically separate from caretaker patter. Keep  ellipsis and white gaps where Japanese leaves floating attribution.
style_sheet.register: Four musics kept apart in modern, speakable English: (1) level literary narration, no archaism despite historical kana; (2) Taki's vague agreeable mumble tipping into false grandiose; (3) wife's brisk Tokyo feminine practicality; (4) workmen's coarse compressed rough-speech. No borrowed English dialect for (4), no poetizing of (2). Formality carried in sentence shape, not thee/thou.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby glosses in source (創作（小説）, 他人《ひと》, 船歌《ナンシー・リー》, 話が止絶《き》れると) signal reading or irony: follow sense in English (e.g. others for 他人) and note only where ironic (boat-song as Nancy Lee). Italics in English only for song titles and for Taki's slogans when cited back as slogans (in one burst!, telephone!).

english: Taki had been thinking of nothing but his creative work, his novel, until it turned oppressive, so he took up his sketch box and went out for a walk — down the stone steps and on wavering down toward the pine wood near the sea. More mindful of passersby than of the view, he left the path and, bending low, hid himself in a thicket of dwarf pines that caught at his head. Then, coming to the broken edge of the hill, he sat cross-legged among the evening primroses. Far off on the sand that shone grey, four or five things like cloths toyed with by the wind were turning in slow circles, and wondering what they could be, he looked up and saw they were the shadows of gulls wheeling low in great rings.

On the hot evening of the second, having finished his board of the distant sea, Taki was trailing blankly home when near the foot of the stone steps he met his wife, who seemed to have been wandering about looking for him.
"Have you just got here? Have you come to visit?"
"I've come to watch them catch the scarlet carp, but they say they just can't catch them!"
"Again... You had better give it up. In the first place, even if you moved them to a pond like that, they would make no show, they would only stink miserably."
"But wasn't it dug on purpose for them? They say it is small but quite deep, so it will be all right!"
"They say that hole was dug because they needed the earth somewhere and had no choice — there seem to be a few goldfish and cheap carp in it, but I think that is just about right."
takes.label: Level narration, live wires (recommended)
takes.line:
The house drafts in this take unless the editor picks another; it is the one that keeps all four registers distinct while letting the narration stay dead level, which is what the crux requires. English that would be wrong for it: any archaising patina; any dialect borrowed from a specific English-speaking place for A and B; any softening of the wife into warmth or hardening of her into shrewishness; elegant variation where the Japanese repeats; and any sentence that tells the reader Taki is ridiculous, since the text never does — it merely lets him order a pond about like a general and then fall half-asleep in the spring breeze of his own importance.

House note, not source evidence: this take was formed from the whole text as given, read once through before drafting; proper names (Taki, Nancy Lee) and the few period song-titles are the only items carried untranslated, and the reading deliberately offers no view on how far Taki is a self-portrait, since the text itself does not settle it and the translation does not need it settled.

english: Taki had grown heavy with thinking of nothing but his fiction, so he shouldered his sketch box and went out for a walk. Down the stone steps, then wavering on down toward the sea, he was halfway through the pine wood near the shore. More mindful of passersby than of the view, he left the little path and, stooping under the dwarf pines that caught at his head, hid himself from sight. Then, coming to a broken edge of the hill, he sat cross legged among the evening primroses. Far away, on the sand gleaming grey, four or five things like cloths tossed by the wind kept circling grandly without pause, and wondering what they could be, he looked up and saw they were the shadows of gulls wheeling low in wide circles.

On the evening of the hot second day, he finished his board of the distant sea, but Taki came drifting back in a daze, and near the foot of the stone steps he met his wife, who seemed to have been wandering about looking for him.
"Have you just got here? Have you come to visit?"
"I've come to watch them catch the scarlet carp, but they say they just can't catch them!"
"Again... They had better give it up. To begin with, even if you took them to a pond like that, they would make no show. They would only stink miserably."
"But wasn't it dug on purpose for that? They say it is small but fairly deep, so it will be all right!"
"I hear that hole was dug because they needed the earth somewhere and could not help it. I hear there are some goldfish and worthless carp in it, but I think that is just about right for it."
takes.label: Sharper satire
takes.line: Narration a touch drier and quicker, Taki's lyric flights rendered with their excess fully audible so the deflations land harder; the wife crisper, the workmen broader. This take makes the comedy unmistakable and would suit readers meeting Makino as a humorist. Its risk is the one named in the crux: a satirical edge in the narration's own diction begins to judge Taki from outside, and the brief sadness of the snow passage — a man who suspects his whole inner life is a botched picture, and flees it — can shrink into a punchline. Wrong for it: caricature; workmen as clowns rather than as the story's only competent people.

english: Taki had grown heavy with thinking of nothing but his creative work, his novel, so with his sketch box in hand he went out for a walk. — Down the stone steps, then on wavering down toward the sea, halfway through the pine wood near the shore. More troubled by passersby than by the view, he left the little path and, stooping, hid himself among the dwarf pines that caught at his head. Then, coming to the broken edge of the hill, he sat cross-legged among the evening primroses. Far off, on the sand that shone grey, four or five things like cloth wrappers toyed with by the wind were solemnly circling, and wondering what they could be he looked up and found them the shadows of gulls wheeling low in great rings.

On the hot evening of the second day he finished his board of the distant sea, yet Taki came trudging blankly home and near the foot of the stone steps met his wife, who seemed to have been loitering there looking for him.
"Just got here? Have you come to visit?"
"I've come to watch them catch the carp, but they say they just can't catch them!"
"Again... They had better give it up. To begin with, carried to a pond like that they would make no show at all, they would only strike the nose pitifully—"
"But wasn't it dug on purpose for that? It is small but they say it is fairly deep, so it will be all right!"
"They say that hole was dug because earth was wanted somewhere and there was no help for it. — It seems there are a few goldfish and worthless carp in it, but I think that is just right."
takes.label: Warmer, more lyrical
takes.line: Narration allowed a dreamier grain, sentences lengthened slightly in the reverie passages, Taki's voice closer to the narrator's so we inhabit the 'dream' before it is punctured; the marriage played with more visible affection, the ending's flatness kept but felt as melancholy. This take honours the fact that the snow vision, however disproportionate, is the most alive writing Taki does in the story. Its risk is ennoblement: prettified, the reveries stop being slightly too much, the carp-hunt loses its mud, and the story becomes a wistful portrait of a dreamer instead of an account of a man whose dreaming is precisely how he avoids everything. Wrong for it: sentimentality about the father and the song; any glow added to the final absence.

options.author: first read (Wonder)
options.case: - The gap between Taki's cherished, unwritten inner work and the squalid, absorbing business that actually fills his days — and the way the narration keeps lending the second the epic language of the first. Taki is a writer who has not really begun: he tells his wife the work is 'about half' done (p28) when in fact, once he took up his pen, he could write it 'in one burst' at any time — or so he believes; putting it into prose feels to him as clumsy and roundabout as making conversation. Everything grand in the story stays in his head, in quotation marks. Everything that actually happens is petty and physical: a pond dug for no good reason, carp that cannot be caught, a house about to be demolished and replaced by a warehouse, a telephone he suddenly decides to sell, carp suddenly worth four hundred yen, creditors at the door. The story's energy is the traffic between the two. His wife's casual remark that his finished seascape looks 'like a snowscape, in midsummer' (p58) detonates a paragraph of self-laceration in which all his realistic fiction and his whole foolish way of living become a botched 'snowscape', a blizzard rises, and he must flee across a white wilderness (p61–62). By section III the same man is bellowing orders at two workmen in a muddy pond like a general, then like an impresario inviting spectators up to the best seats, then discovering that this is more fun than any pleasure he knows (p165–179). In section IV the pumping-out of the pond, done by his assembled creditors, acquires 'the same underlying force as the chorus of Nancy Lee' (p210) — the sentimental whaling song he inherited from his father — while Taki himself is simply absent, gone to Tokyo 'to buy a lamp' (p212). If a translation resolves this into satire on a lazy writer, or into lyrical sympathy for a dreamer, it has chosen one pole and lost the story. For the English: Keep the comic disproportion intact. Do not make Taki's inner language beautiful and the pond business merely coarse background, and do not make the narration wink at him from outside. The same English must be able to inflate a carp-hunt into a battle, a chorus, a theatrical tableau, and then let it collapse into mud, cicadas and an unpaid bill. His quoted-back phrases — “the difficult work I'm holding in my head!”, “in one burst!”, “Nancy Lee”, “the telephone!”, “the terrifying blizzard!”, “nothing but a snowscape to look at!” — should recur recognisably, because in p160 the narration throws his own slogans back at him as they all scatter 'like goose down' while he sits glaring at the pond.
options.tradeoff: One crux, broadly framed: it preserves both poles and forbids a verdict, but gives no specific instruction on the workmen's vernacular or Taki's imitation of it.

options.author: crux check (Wonder)
options.case:
- TAKI SEES THE WORLD IN REVERSE SEASON: HIS 'FINISHED' SUMMER SEASCAPE LOOKS — RIGHTLY — LIKE A SNOWSCAPE, BECAUSE HE LIVES IN AN UNWRITTEN, 'HELD-IN-THE-HEAD' FANTASY AND IS BLIND TO WHAT IS IN FRONT OF HIM. THE WIFE'S CASUAL LINE IN p58 TRIGGERS NOT EMBARRASSMENT BUT A FULL MID-SUMMER BLIZZARD HALLUCINATION IN p61-62 (OWL'S EYES IN DAYLIGHT, BURIED UNDER SIN-FUL SNOW 'AS LARGE AS PEONY PETALS'). THE SAME WORDS KEEP RECURRING — 架空 MADE OF AIR, 夢, 'IN ONE BREATH' (p28, p74-75), THE SIX-DAY JOB HE MUST ONLY 'HOLD IN HIS HEAD' (p135, p160) — AND IN p160 THE NARRATOR LISTS THEM BACK VERBATIM TO SHOW THEM ALL SCATTERED 'LIKE GOOSE DOWN' THE MOMENT MONEY APPEARS. THAT MAKES THE TITLE AN INDICTMENT, NOT A MOOD. For the English: KEEP THE SNOW LITERAL, SUDDEN AND UNEXPLAINED, AND KEEP A RIGID CONCORDANCE FOR THE REPEATED PHRASES — 'in one breath/at one go,' 'hold it in my head,' 'Nancy Lee,' 'telephone,' 'terrible blizzard,' 'snowscape' — SO THE CATALOGUE IN p160 LANDS AS SELF-QUOTATION. DO NOT SMOOTH THE SUMMER/SNOW INVERSION INTO A SIMILE FOR HIS STATE OF MIND.
- THE COMEDY AND THE VERDICT ARE IN THE COLLISION OF REGISTERS: LYRICAL, MOCK-HEROIC NARRATION OF A MUDDY POND-SIEGE AGAINST THE WORKMEN'S VULGAR DIALECT — AND TAKI, WHO CLAIMED NO FEELING FOR ANYTHING (p18), BECOMES A SHOUTING, TABLE-THUMPING 'GRAND BOURGEOIS' (p160) THE INSTANT THE DESPISED CARP ARE WORTH ¥400. A AND B SPEAK IN HEAVILY ELIDED, ROUGH VERNACULAR (p40-47, WITH THE NARRATOR EVEN GLOSSING 手前え AS 'FIRST PERSON'), AND THEIR BODIES — DRAGON AND UNFINISHED HANNYA TATTOOS (p48) — ARE GIVEN THE EPIC DESCRIPTION TAKI'S OWN WORK NEVER GETS. THE POND BATTLE (p154-193) IS NARRATED AS WARFARE, THEN UNDER-CUT BY 'A WATER-FIGHT ON A HOT DAY.' TAKI FIRST EAVESDROPS, THEN IMITATES A'S CADENCE, ORDERS THE CARP BEATEN TO DEATH (p173), AND BY p210 HIS CREDITORS ARE PUMPING THE POND TO THE RHYTHM OF NANCY LEE'S CHORUS WHILE HE IS ABSENT IN TOKYO BUYING A LAMP. For the English: KEEP THREE REGISTERS SHARPLY APART IN PLAIN, SPEAKABLE ENGLISH: HIS EVASIVE MUMBLE AND FALSE GRANDIOSES, THE WIFE'S BRISK DOMESTIC LOGIC, AND THE WORKMEN'S COARSE, COMPRESSED ROUGH-SPEECH (WITHOUT EYE-DIALECT CARICATURE). ABOVE ALL KEEP TAKI'S SLIDE INTO IMITATION OF A (p165-176) BRUTAL AND COMIC — IT MUST SOUND LIKE A DIFFERENT MAN FROM THE 'SNOWSCAPE' REVERIE, NOT A POLISHED NARRATOR SUMMARISING.
options.tradeoff: Two cruxes, narrowly framed: it adds rigid concordance, literal snow and a distinct register crux, but hardens the story into an indictment/verdict that the other reading expressly forbids.

fork.question: Do they name the same thing in different words, or different things? They overlap on the unwritten-work/pond traffic, the snowscape detonation, the recurring slogans and the Nancy Lee pond scenes, but they are not the same crux restated: Option 0 makes the refusal to judge Taki the crux itself, while Option 1 makes judgement — title as indictment, comedy as verdict — and the three-register collision, including Taki's imitation of the workmen, separate cruxes. Choosing between them decides both the book's tone toward Taki and whether dialect/register is a load-bearing translation rule or a by-product of comic disproportion, and that choice will recur on every page; the text as quoted does not settle it, since the same scenes (p58–62, p160, p165–210) are cited by both sides for opposite tonal conclusions. Recommendation: proceed on Option 0 until the editor rules, because it contains Option 1's evidence without pre-deciding the verdict or a rigid concordance, whereas proceeding on Option 1 would bake a satirical stance and phrase-freezing into the draft that would be expensive to undo if the editor prefers the open reading.

head.say: FORK: The two readers substantially overlap but name different cruxes — Option 0's crux is the unresolved traffic between Taki's unwritten inner work and the petty business that borrows its epic language, with an express bar on resolving it into satire or sympathy; Option 1 adds a second, distinct crux in the collision of three registers and Taki's imitation of the workmen, hardens the snowscape/title into an indictment and a verdict, and imposes rigid concordance. I therefore do not pick: this is not one better than the other, it is a recurring question of tone and of whether register is itself load-bearing, and the scenes both cite (p58–62, p160, p165–210) support either tonal conclusion. I open a fork and recommend the run proceed on Option 0 in the meantime, since it preserves both poles and all the shared evidence without locking in the indictment or the concordance, which would be costly to reverse.

second.say: CONFIDENCE: HIGH ON BOTH. WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: EVIDENCE IN THE JAPANESE THAT THE REPEATED PHRASES I CALL DELIBERATE ECHOES ARE UNMARKED STOCK PHRASES WITH NO RETURN-VALUE IN p160 WOULD DEMOTE THE FIRST FROM A CRUX TO ORDINARY CONSISTENCY OF TERMINOLOGY.

body.why: This short story totals well under one reading limit and its four numbered sections form a single continuous arc, with the final section too brief to judge alone, so it is best held whole as one part.

open_questions.question: What exactly has Taki produced in the 'finished' sketch, and how literally should the snow vision be taken? The text never shows us the picture; we have only his wife's puzzled remark and his disproportionate reaction. Is the sketch a failed seascape, an accidental near-abstract, or an honest rendering of how dazzled eyes see a midsummer shore? The translation should preserve the fact that we never see it directly — but the degree of visual oddity implied in 'like a snowscape' affects how strange the English should let the phrase sound.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The title hangs on this unseen picture. Over-explaining it (a bad painting, a visionary one, a hallucination) settles the story's central uncertainty.

open_questions.question: How much of the father's whaling-ship past is family myth? The father 'said' he shipped on a whaler in his American schooldays and learned Nancy Lee from the sailors; Taki repeats this as fact, but the whole anecdote has the shine of a story told too often and too theatrically, with gestures. Should the English keep a faint hearsay colouring ('he used to say...') or report it straight?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The song, and the father's romantic self-image, are Taki's one inherited piece of 'the sea'; whether he is heir to an adventure or to a performance bears on how we hear his own performances in section III.

open_questions.question: Is Taki's final absence from the pumping of the pond evasion, indifference, or the story's quiet verdict — that the work of his life will be done by other people, for money he owes, while he is elsewhere on an errand? The last line gives only the caretaker's report ('gone to Tokyo to buy a lamp'). Should the English let that stand as flatly as the Japanese does, with no closing cadence supplied?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Any added point or rounding-off in the final sentence would manufacture an ending the text refuses; but how bare 'to buy a lamp' sounds in English decides whether the refusal reads as design or as a translation gap.

open_questions.question: Why do Taki and his wife live in separate houses, and what is the temperature of the marriage? The text gives only glancing evidence: she comes looking for him, teases him, fears he will join the workmen's drinking, rings the caretaker to intercept him. Is this estrangement, a workable arrangement, or a wife managing a hopeless husband at arm's length?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Her lines can be played cold, affectionate or exasperated, and English dialogue will force a choice line by line; the reading above assumes affection worn into exasperation, but the text never confirms it.

body.reading:
The crux comes first. Taki lives by a phrase: 'in one burst!' (一気呵勢, p74). It is his motto, his excuse and his sedative — having thought it, he can become 'easily optimistic', make himself a little more leisure, and sink back into the 'dream'. The story is built as a series of occasions on which that leisure gets filled by something else, each time more completely. First a walk to escape the oppressiveness of thinking about fiction (p2); then his wife's arrival and the long, circling conversation about the carp, the doomed house, the trip they will supposedly take, the house they will supposedly rent in Tokyo (p3–p48); then the detonation of the 'snowscape' remark; then drink, the telephone inspiration, the carp valuation, the brothel; then the hunt itself, which swallows an entire day and remakes him as 'a haughty bourgeois waiting for his prey' (p160); finally the creditors pumping the pond dry in heroic unison while he is not there. Nothing in his life is ever quite refused — the trip is always about to happen, his mother may join them whenever she likes, the work is always half done — and the English must keep that soft, agreeable evasiveness in the dialogue. Taki's characteristic move is the answer that sounds like agreement and commits him to nothing ('Go if you like', p30, at once corrected, too late, to 'I want to go'), and the narration itself notices the habit (p33). If his lines are made decisive, or his wife's made merely nagging, the marriage — two people who have long practice at not quite meeting — disappears.

Register is where a fluent draft will most reliably go wrong, because the text runs on at least four distinct musics and keeps cutting between them without warning. There is the narration in a literary Taishō-Shōwa written style, capable of a level, almost reportorial calm (the opening walk, the still noon tableau of p180–181, where the two workmen freeze like figures in a play and a bubble bursts on the mud). There is Taki's interior weather: rhymed, 'poetic' reverie (韻文的な想ひ) that tips without a seam into self-parody — the snow passage of p61–62 is the extreme case, moving from an owl's eyes in daylight to sinful snowflakes 'the size of peony petals' burying his body, all triggered by a wife's mild puzzlement and punctured at once by her 'What's the matter?' and his sheepish change of subject (p63–66). There is the wife's speech: quick, Tokyo, feminine in the period's inflections, teasing and managerial at once, the only voice in the story that consistently says what things cost and what will actually happen. And there are A and B, the tattooed workmen, whose pond-side talk (p40–47) is broad working-class vernacular — boastful, sweaty, obscene round the edges — set down with evident relish by the narrator, who even pauses to describe their tattoos (the completed dragon; the unfinished hannya mask, and Taki's unasked question about why it was abandoned, p48). The temptation is to level these into one pleasant literary voice, or to render the workmen in some borrowed English dialect that pins them to a place they never lived. Resist both. They should sound rougher, faster and funnier than everyone else without turning into music-hall turns; Taki should sound smoother and vaguer than everyone else without turning into a poet.

The comedy is deadpan and structural, and it lives in repetition. Catch the carp: the word つかまへる tolls through the story from the wife's first line (p5) through the workmen's laments to Taki's bellowing 'the net! the net! the net!' (p166), and the pond obligingly clouds every time anyone moves — a small, perfect mechanism of frustration that the English should let recur in the same plain words rather than varying into 'grab', 'land', 'net' by turns. Likewise 'in one burst', which migrates grotesquely from Taki's unwritten masterpiece (p74) to A and B's plan to pump the pond dry 'in one burst' (p206): the same slogan, finally attached to the only decisive act in the book, performed by his creditors. Nancy Lee travels the same road, from the father's deck-song, through Taki's solitary whistling and his wife's ostentatious ear-covering (p104–106), to the straining chorus of the pump-handlers (p210) — the one moment of genuine collective vigour in the story, and it belongs to the men he owes money. Keep the song's title untranslated and unexplained in the text; its slight foreign quaintness in 1927 Japan is part of the point, and the wife's objection that an American sailors' song is old and vulgar should be allowed to stand against Taki's sentimentality without the narration adjudicating. The same deadpan applies to money, which a fluent version may be tempted to keep vague: ten yen produced from a wife's purse, four hundred yen for carp, month-end bills, the telephone as a saleable asset. The amounts are the story's ballast.

What the text leaves unsaid should stay unsaid. Subjects drop for sentences at a time; dialogue goes unattributed (notably the restaurant haggling, p108–120, and the drunken walk home, p121–146, where Taki's parenthesised realisations — the telephone! it's mine! I'll sell it! — interrupt the old caretaker's patter and should stay typographically and rhythmically separate, a drunk man's lightning inside a slow scene). The unfinished things are thematic, not accidental: the unfinished tattoo, the unfinished house extension meant perhaps for a Buddhist altar room (p76), the unwritten novel, the uncaught carp, the trip untaken. A translation that completes sentences, assigns speakers the Japanese leaves floating, or explains why B stopped the tattoo has committed Berman's clarification in exactly the place this text forbids it. Equally, do not prettify the imagery in the lyrical passages: 'sinful snow-shavings', an owl's eyes in the light, 'goose-down' scattering of his grand phrases — these are meant to be a little too much, and their excess, kept, is what makes the puncturing funny and then, briefly, sad.

A note on limits: the period surface (historical kana, Taishō diction) should not be answered with English archaism. Taki's world — buses, telephones, restaurants, harmonicas playing 'Ai Ai Ai' and 'Valencia', a Tokyo March — was modern to itself. The English should be modern enough to let the comedy move, with its formality carried in sentence shape rather than in thee-and-thou colouring. I cannot settle from the text alone how far Makino intends Taki as self-portrait, and the reading does not need it: the narration's evenness — it never once calls him lazy, dishonest or absurd outright — works whether the target is the author, a friend, or a type. That evenness is the final thing to protect. The last scene's heroic chorus and the absent hero are presented in the same level voice as everything else; the English should end as flatly as it began.
body.say: Reading (prose, crux first), open questions, and voice takes for Makino Shin'ichi's “Snowscape” (雪景色, 1927).

second_crux.for_the_english: KEEP THE SNOW LITERAL, SUDDEN AND UNEXPLAINED, AND KEEP A RIGID CONCORDANCE FOR THE REPEATED PHRASES — 'in one breath/at one go,' 'hold it in my head,' 'Nancy Lee,' 'telephone,' 'terrible blizzard,' 'snowscape' — SO THE CATALOGUE IN p160 LANDS AS SELF-QUOTATION. DO NOT SMOOTH THE SUMMER/SNOW INVERSION INTO A SIMILE FOR HIS STATE OF MIND.
second_crux.point: TAKI SEES THE WORLD IN REVERSE SEASON: HIS 'FINISHED' SUMMER SEASCAPE LOOKS — RIGHTLY — LIKE A SNOWSCAPE, BECAUSE HE LIVES IN AN UNWRITTEN, 'HELD-IN-THE-HEAD' FANTASY AND IS BLIND TO WHAT IS IN FRONT OF HIM.
second_crux.why: THE WIFE'S CASUAL LINE IN p58 TRIGGERS NOT EMBARRASSMENT BUT A FULL MID-SUMMER BLIZZARD HALLUCINATION IN p61-62 (OWL'S EYES IN DAYLIGHT, BURIED UNDER SIN-FUL SNOW 'AS LARGE AS PEONY PETALS'). THE SAME WORDS KEEP RECURRING — 架空 MADE OF AIR, 夢, 'IN ONE BREATH' (p28, p74-75), THE SIX-DAY JOB HE MUST ONLY 'HOLD IN HIS HEAD' (p135, p160) — AND IN p160 THE NARRATOR LISTS THEM BACK VERBATIM TO SHOW THEM ALL SCATTERED 'LIKE GOOSE DOWN' THE MOMENT MONEY APPEARS. THAT MAKES THE TITLE AN INDICTMENT, NOT A MOOD.

second_crux.for_the_english: KEEP THREE REGISTERS SHARPLY APART IN PLAIN, SPEAKABLE ENGLISH: HIS EVASIVE MUMBLE AND FALSE GRANDIOSES, THE WIFE'S BRISK DOMESTIC LOGIC, AND THE WORKMEN'S COARSE, COMPRESSED ROUGH-SPEECH (WITHOUT EYE-DIALECT CARICATURE). ABOVE ALL KEEP TAKI'S SLIDE INTO IMITATION OF A (p165-176) BRUTAL AND COMIC — IT MUST SOUND LIKE A DIFFERENT MAN FROM THE 'SNOWSCAPE' REVERIE, NOT A POLISHED NARRATOR SUMMARISING.
second_crux.point: THE COMEDY AND THE VERDICT ARE IN THE COLLISION OF REGISTERS: LYRICAL, MOCK-HEROIC NARRATION OF A MUDDY POND-SIEGE AGAINST THE WORKMEN'S VULGAR DIALECT — AND TAKI, WHO CLAIMED NO FEELING FOR ANYTHING (p18), BECOMES A SHOUTING, TABLE-THUMPING 'GRAND BOURGEOIS' (p160) THE INSTANT THE DESPISED CARP ARE WORTH ¥400.
second_crux.why: A AND B SPEAK IN HEAVILY ELIDED, ROUGH VERNACULAR (p40-47, WITH THE NARRATOR EVEN GLOSSING 手前え AS 'FIRST PERSON'), AND THEIR BODIES — DRAGON AND UNFINISHED HANNYA TATTOOS (p48) — ARE GIVEN THE EPIC DESCRIPTION TAKI'S OWN WORK NEVER GETS. THE POND BATTLE (p154-193) IS NARRATED AS WARFARE, THEN UNDER-CUT BY 'A WATER-FIGHT ON A HOT DAY.' TAKI FIRST EAVESDROPS, THEN IMITATES A'S CADENCE, ORDERS THE CARP BEATEN TO DEATH (p173), AND BY p210 HIS CREDITORS ARE PUMPING THE POND TO THE RHYTHM OF NANCY LEE'S CHORUS WHILE HE IS ABSENT IN TOKYO BUYING A LAMP.

voice_takes.label: Level narration, live wires (recommended)
voice_takes.line:
The house drafts in this take unless the editor picks another; it is the one that keeps all four registers distinct while letting the narration stay dead level, which is what the crux requires. English that would be wrong for it: any archaising patina; any dialect borrowed from a specific English-speaking place for A and B; any softening of the wife into warmth or hardening of her into shrewishness; elegant variation where the Japanese repeats; and any sentence that tells the reader Taki is ridiculous, since the text never does — it merely lets him order a pond about like a general and then fall half-asleep in the spring breeze of his own importance.

House note, not source evidence: this take was formed from the whole text as given, read once through before drafting; proper names (Taki, Nancy Lee) and the few period song-titles are the only items carried untranslated, and the reading deliberately offers no view on how far Taki is a self-portrait, since the text itself does not settle it and the translation does not need it settled.

voice_takes.label: Sharper satire
voice_takes.line: Narration a touch drier and quicker, Taki's lyric flights rendered with their excess fully audible so the deflations land harder; the wife crisper, the workmen broader. This take makes the comedy unmistakable and would suit readers meeting Makino as a humorist. Its risk is the one named in the crux: a satirical edge in the narration's own diction begins to judge Taki from outside, and the brief sadness of the snow passage — a man who suspects his whole inner life is a botched picture, and flees it — can shrink into a punchline. Wrong for it: caricature; workmen as clowns rather than as the story's only competent people.

voice_takes.label: Warmer, more lyrical
voice_takes.line: Narration allowed a dreamier grain, sentences lengthened slightly in the reverie passages, Taki's voice closer to the narrator's so we inhabit the 'dream' before it is punctured; the marriage played with more visible affection, the ending's flatness kept but felt as melancholy. This take honours the fact that the snow vision, however disproportionate, is the most alive writing Taki does in the story. Its risk is ennoblement: prettified, the reveries stop being slightly too much, the carp-hunt loses its mud, and the story becomes a wistful portrait of a dreamer instead of an account of a man whose dreaming is precisely how he avoids everything. Wrong for it: sentimentality about the father and the song; any glow added to the final absence.

revision.english: I

Taki had been thinking of nothing but his creative work, his novel, until it turned oppressive, so he took up his sketch box and went out for a walk — down the stone steps and on wavering down toward the pine wood near the sea. More mindful of passersby than of the view, he left the path and, bending low, hid himself in a thicket of dwarf pines that caught at his head. Then, coming to the broken edge of the hill, he sat cross-legged among the evening primroses. Far off on the sand that shone grey, four or five things like cloths toyed with by the wind were turning in slow circles, and wondering what they could be, he looked up and saw they were the shadows of gulls wheeling low in great rings.
notes: Kept the single long movement of hiding, sitting, and mistaking shadows; evening primrose for 月見草.

revision.english: On the hot evening of the second, having finished his board of the distant sea, Taki was trailing blankly home when near the foot of the stone steps he met his wife, who seemed to have been wandering about looking for him.
"Have you just got here? Have you come to visit?"
notes: Taken as Taki to his wife, from the meeting in p3.

revision.english: "I've come to watch them catch the scarlet carp, but they say they just can't catch them!"
notes: Hi-goi kept as scarlet carp; catch kept plain for the tolling verb.

revision.english: "Again... You had better give it up. In the first place, even if you moved them to a pond like that, they would make no show, they would only stink miserably."
"But wasn't it dug on purpose for them? They say it is small but quite deep, so it will be all right!"
"They say that hole was dug because they needed the earth somewhere and had no choice — there seem to be a few goldfish and cheap carp in it, but I think that is just about right."
notes: Cheap carp for 駄鯉, to keep the low value against the later valuation.

revision.english: "But it's no use leaving them here, is it? If somebody was going to live here that would be one thing, but they're going to clear it all away and before long some warehouse or other is going to be built here, isn't that the story — or have you got some idea of your own?"
"No —" Taki laughed.
"If you haven't, then keep quiet, do. It's strange, you're oddly cold about anything that's just there —"

"Here too —" she said, looking up at the house showing through the mandarin trees, amused for no reason in particular. "They say at last it's going to be cleared away before long. You must feel flat. It won't fetch a penny!"
notes: "won't fetch a penny" for 一文にもならない: literally not worth a mon, kept as small money.

revision.english: "There's hardly any memories in this house, for me —" That was the sort of thing Taki said.
"But still, this makes a clean break for you. At last it's over, isn't it?"
"I suppose so —"

"So the scarlet carp are what's left!" she murmured as if to herself. "Even if you thought of grilling them, there's not a single pot in this house — and yet don't you feel the least bit sentimental, about the carp, for instance?"
notes: 焼けない: I take it as grilling the carp to eat, there being no utensils in the house to be cleared; it could also point to burning the house itself, which context does not settle.

revision.english: "For some reason —" Taki said with an earnest, composed air. "I feel nothing, so little that I worry even myself —"
"That must be because you're getting into your own work bit by bit. Splendid."
"Mm."
"You don't grumble the way you used to lately — Mother said that reassures her more than anything, she was delighted."
"Delighted!"

It's all very well to set her mind at rest, but even in front of Mother, though nobody really believes a word of it anyway, to come out with such hollow things... it's embarrassing, for us! No ordinary hollowness, but something wildly off the scale, like a dream, something outrageous...
What I said, I don't know, I've forgotten! But I've told no lies—

You don't know the words that make a listener feel solemn. When it comes to saying something to comfort other people, you come out with something wildly grand— but well, anything is better, I suppose, than grumbling and sulking!
notes: Kept ruby reading of 他人 as 'other people' rather than 'another person'.

revision.english: Was she so eloquent whenever they met because they lived in separate houses? Or was it some kind of irony? Taki wondered.
That doesn't matter at all. More to the point, is your work coming along? You seem very hard at it.
notes: 勉強 as his creative work, not school study.

revision.english: "About half—" he blurted out, as if with nothing to weigh on him— He had of late been absorbed in the conception of a wholly imaginary story. Once he took up his pen, half or nothing, he thought he could write it off in one burst! at any time. No, writing itself gave him no concern. At times he was even dazzled into oppressiveness by too unbridled imaginings, but to take up his pen and turn it into prose, just as when exchanging words with other people, with clumsy phrasing going the long way round, fell short of his fine inspiration.
notes: Kept fixed slogan 'in one burst!' for 一気呵勢; kept second 他人 as 'other people' per ruby.

revision.english: When that's done, will we really go on the trip?
Go if you like.
notes: Kept deliberately noncommittal agreement; corrected too late in p32.

revision.english: "Go if you like"! It was you who brought it up first, long ago.
So we'll go. I want to go.
Getting the words across wrong like that, against his own intention, was one of his habits.
"What I think doesn't count, does it, or else as usual we'll end up not going."
"Not this time, surely —. You do the thinking. I don't know anywhere, so anywhere is bound to feel new and amusing. We might as well go meaning to settle."
notes: Kept the soft evasiveness: proposal left to her, commitment to nothing.

revision.english: "Talk of settling sounds oppressive. Anyway, we'll have to find a rented house, some time. Tokyo again?"
"Tokyo would be good."
"Mother says she doesn't mind joining us any time, but if you come there there'll be no study, will there?"
"As for having no study, I've got used to that from my Tokyo life till now."

Talking this over as they came round into the garden, they found two workmen settled on the veranda, stripped bare with their headbands knotted to the front. Wiping sweat and drinking tea, the two were lamenting that the carp simply could not be caught. Looking down at the reddish brown water, A folded his arms: "It clouds straight up like this—"
notes: Workmen for 鳢職, bare with headbands for 向う鉞巻の裸体; reddish brown for 赧土色. Dialect normalized to rough plain speech without borrowed dialect.

revision.english: "It's no use, they're thoroughly shy now. The moment we put one foot in, they start thrashing first and cloud it all up!" B said, frowning.
notes: Kept catch and cloud in plain words for the repeated mechanism.

revision.english: "At this rate it won't clear back to what it was till the day after tomorrow or so."
notes: Left unattributed as in Japanese; speaker floats between A and B.

revision.english: "Shall we just go at them blind, one more push!"
notes: Left unattributed as in Japanese.

revision.english: "Once it's like this, aim or nothing, there's nothing to go by."
notes: Left unattributed as in Japanese.

revision.english: "I went and tumbled right into the trap, so it's not the heat. My arse is grazed raw all over! The water's going to soak in, isn't it?"
notes: Source glosses teme'e in a bracketed note as first person; rendered simply as I since English needs no gloss.
Exact dialect force uncertain; taken as a fall into the fish trap leaving scraped buttocks that pond water will sting.

revision.english: "It's a queerer job than you'd think, this is. Damn silly and it works you to the bone. My head's gone muzzy with it!"
"Looks like we'll have to go and fetch a tradesman. If we just catch at them blind we'll kill them, and then there'll be nothing left for it!"
notes: 'tradesman' for shobainin, kept vague as Taki has not yet understood it means the goldfish man in p49.
'catch' kept for the concordance verb tsukamaeru.

revision.english: A's was a splendid tattoo, a fine dragon striking a pose across his whole back, with terrible wheeling clouds spreading their wings to the tips of both arms. B's, for some reason, looked to have been left off before it was finished, only the outline of a hannya mask traced at about eight tenths on the bare skin. Taki had sometimes thought of asking B why he had stopped at that, but it felt somehow wrong, and he had held back.
notes: 'hannya mask' and 'eight tenths' kept literal; the reason for stopping is withheld in the source and left so.

revision.english: As he walked straight through to the inner room and opened the lid of his sketch box, the men's shrill talk came sharply to Taki's ears. Catch! Catch! — their words took his interest, and he thought, so there are tradesmen who make a trade of catching fish, then? Only later did he realise this had meant the goldfish man.
notes: 'tradesman' kept as in p47 to preserve Taki's vagueness before the later realisation.
'Catch! Catch!' keeps tsukamaeru in the same plain verb used throughout.

revision.english: "Is that what you've been painting?"
"Mm."
Then his wife said, in the most straightforward tone, "It's not finished yet, is it."
Taki blinked for a moment, unnaturally, then said with forced decisiveness, "No, this is finished as it stands."
So saying, arms folded, he leaned his upper body back and stared hard at the picture with faint eyes.
notes: Kept faint eyes literal for 微かな眼; it reads stiff in English but marks his strained pose after insisting the sketch is finished.

revision.english: "So?" she seemed to murmur without meaning to. And then, "Somehow it looks like a snowscape, though it's midsummer—" she said critically.
notes: Grouped p57 with p58: p57 is only a lead-in to her remark in p58. Kept snowscape as a hard noun and kept the trailing dash found in the Japanese.

revision.english: Taki flushed suddenly and muttered something under his breath. For the first time his wife wondered if she had said something wrong.

It had lately become rare for Taki to mind what others said. — As if waking with his nerves strangely warped, he was seized by an unpleasant cold. His own eyes were an owl's eyes in daylight! He fell into such self-mockery. Drunk only on vague reveries, how much sorrow must his very existence be giving to the hearts of those around him, he ran even to such feeble, plausible worries. And the realistic novels he had written until now, and the buoyant and foolish way he had conducted himself in this world, all of it turned into a clumsy, mistake-ridden 'snowscape', and then at once a terrifying blizzard rose, and closing his eyes and bowing his chest he had no choice but to flee headlong into the white wilderness, able to see nothing....
notes: Kept the excess literal: owl's eyes in daylight, terrifying blizzard, white wilderness. Single quotes for 'snowscape' mark it as his own word thrown back at him. One dash only, where the Japanese has one.

revision.english: "Ah..." Before he could even utter a groan, great sinful flakes of snow as large as peony petals came thickly down and in a moment buried his whole body.
notes: Kept sinful flakes and peony petals literal and slightly too much, as written; not smoothed into a simile for his feelings.

revision.english: "What's the matter?"
"Eh?"

"I'm not angry. — The country is all very well, but at dusk it is unbearably lonely! It's horribly hot and close. I wonder if I should go and lend a hand with that or something—" he said, forcing a wry smile.
notes: Dashes only where the Japanese has them. Forced smile for 事更に苦笑: a deliberate change of subject after the reverie.

revision.english: "Stop it — you're strange."
"Something bumped into my leg!"
notes: Speaker left floating in the Japanese, as with the pond-side talk throughout; kept unattributed.

revision.english: "Whoa! Deep, deep here."
In the muddy water of the dusk, the sight of the two tattooed men raging about like madmen struck Taki as eerie.
notes: Kurikara monmon is tattoo slang, here used for the two workmen in general; rendered plainly as tattooed men without specifying dragon or hannya, which the text distinguishes only in p48.

revision.english: II

That day too they kept up their noise in the pond until dusk, but it was failure again. Clicking their tongues in vexation, they withdrew to the caretaking old couple's sitting room and, with no thought of going back to their own homes, began to drink.

Taki lay face up in the middle of the empty, bare room, gazing at the ceiling. By day, if only the weather was fair, he went to the sea and did nothing but swim. He never tired of giving himself up to groundless, verselike reveries, but with thoughts of money coming to mind he muttered that he might soon make a start on his work.
notes: Kakuu ni inbun-teki na omoi: kept literal as groundless and verselike to hold the interior register apart from narration, without poetizing.

revision.english: "In one burst!"
notes: Ikki kasei kept to the fixed concordance in one burst throughout, from unwritten work to pond pumping.

revision.english: It had become like a pet phrase with him, and with the thought he easily turned optimistic, made himself a little more leisure, and sank deeper into the 'dream'.
notes: Yume kept quoted as 'dream' to mark it as his slogan word recurring to p160.

revision.english: And he, growing drowsy, showed no sign of readily withdrawing to his own room. The room Taki had fixed upon as his study had, for some reason, never been wired for electric light. An extension left half begun and abandoned these four or five years, it had, one gathered, been meant perhaps for an altar room. To recover his long reversed day and night, he had rather welcomed this and had left unlit there alone the light that could easily have been drawn in. And only in the daytime, and then very rarely, for he was unused to it, on cloudy days when he could not go to the sea, did he sit at his desk. When night came on, half out of eccentricity, he would read by the light of an oil lamp or a candlestand, or give himself to musings truly foolish as a 'snowscape.'
notes: 'Altar room' renders what the bible takes to be a Buddhist altar room extension; the passage only conjectures its purpose. 'Snowscape' kept hard to hold the concordance with p58 and p160.

revision.english: "What shall we do about dinner?"
notes: Speaker unstated; taken as the wife from the exchange that follows.

revision.english: "Here will do. Order something?"
notes: Taken as Taki answering.

revision.english: "It has grown dark, so walk me as far as town while you see me off. For once I want to eat somewhere else. And I have a little money on me today."

Hearing that, Taki agreed on the spot. His wife, with the revelry next door growing livelier by the minute, all for trying other means next carp day and making a quick catch before the water clouded, for taking the long view —
notes: Second sentence left incomplete as in the Japanese, closing with the dash where p81 and p82 break in as the voices from the next room. 'Catch' kept for the concordance.

revision.english: "Once it is clouded, it is more than our hands can manage, whatever you say! Ha ha ha..."
notes: Speaker left floating between A and B as in the Japanese; rough workmen's speech kept plain, without borrowed dialect. 'Clouded' kept for the clouding water concordance.

revision.english: "It truly nettles me, I cannot bear it. Come to this, it is pride. I cannot wait patiently for the water to clear."
notes: Speaker left floating as in the Japanese. 'Clear' kept against 'clouded' in p81.

revision.english: Troubled that Taki had apparently been listening to such high-spirited voices for some time, she urged him to set out. She feared that if she went away he would be sure to join their drinking. That Taki, given any chance, would take up with people of quite another sort and put on a foolish revel, the very thought of it was more than she could bear.
notes: 畑違ひ kept as 'of quite another sort' to keep class difference without fixing a trade; the last clause leaves her disgust general, as the Japanese does.

revision.english: They waited for the bus that came by the hour, but it would not readily come, so talking again of the trip and other things they walked along the avenue of pines in the moonlight.
“The feeling of midsummer is only a very brief moment between July and August, I think.”

“When you put it that way, once we are into August the nights feel more like autumn. But thinking in that way, in winter or in spring too there are only a few days that are truly the peak. The whole year is just the seasons shifting past one another.”
“That is true...”
“After this it must be the night in any case. With that light in that room it will never do, will it?”
notes: I take this to mean night work in his unlit study as days shorten, but the Japanese leaves the implication unstated, so I keep it flat.

revision.english: “Is it not all right as it is?”
“That sort of mood...”
“No, however autumnal it gets, this time I mean to give up the night altogether.”
notes: 夜は絶対に止める: whether he means night work or staying up is not settled; I keep 'the night' literal rather than choosing.

revision.english: When talk came to a stop she took a harmonica from inside her sash and walked along playing it. She had no other accomplishment to speak of, but strangely she was skillful at this. And from time to time she picked up the popular tunes from her middle school brother and others and practiced them eagerly. Lately she had mastered rather difficult pieces (?), such things as “Ai Ai Ai” and “Valencia” and “Light Cavalry.”
notes: 帯の間 rendered as 'inside her sash' per style sheet; song titles kept as transliteration; (?) kept to carry the narrator's ironic query on 難曲.

revision.english: "Let's hear the Tokyo March."
"You do love that one, don't you — like the old sports days —"
notes: Fragmentary in the Japanese; left as a trailing-off tease.

revision.english: "...Good! — And next, American Patrol."
"You know a lot, don't you! — Right..."
"...Good! Good! I couldn't do that even by whistling. ...Now next — well! What shall I ask for?"

Taki, in the freshest of spirits, was casting about for the next number, when his wife, as if she found his ordering tiresome, as if she had not taken it out to answer his requests at all but to beguile her own solitude as she pleased — said in a throwaway voice, "No Nancy Lee, thank you," and fell to practising "Mori no Kajiya," which Taki did not know.
notes: Joined as one English paragraph: p98 breaks off on a dash leading straight into her words in p99. Song-titles kept as in house style; Mori no Kajiya left romanised as Taki does not know it.

revision.english: "What's this, stealing a march on me like that. Who said, play me Nancy Lee!"
In fact when he was at a loss what to hear, knowing few tunes, what Taki always came to at once was "Nancy Lee."
"Rude, always marking me down for that."
She seemed not to hear his muttering at all.

Nancy Lee was the 'whistling' Taki's dead father had taught them. His father used to say he had picked it up from the sailors there when, back in his schooldays in America, he had used the summer holidays to ship aboard a whaler. He used to say the sailors working on deck would fall to humming Nancy Lee at the least thing. Having taken to the whaler so badly that he had once thrown everything aside to work as one of its sailors, the father, when talk turned to the sea, in his pride and absorption loved to repeat his reminiscences with bold gestures, making the 'boat-song' Nancy Lee his refrain.
notes: Kept hearsay colouring with 'used to say' twice, as text repeats with だと云った; kept 'boat-song' with Nancy Lee to show ruby gloss.

revision.english: Taki was taken, beyond its simple cheerfulness, with the strain in which a peculiar, faintly lingering sweet-and-bitter plaint seemed to drift, and even now it survived as his habit whenever he whistled. Apart from that he had almost nothing he could whistle.

She, on the grounds that its pathos was sickly-sweet to the point of blatancy and that the passages like a shouted chorus were forced, and out of a contrary taste that held an American sailors' song old and vulgar, claimed Taki's unconscious whistling got on her nerves and would cover her ears. Hauling in the rigging, taking the helm, racing up the mast — the accompanying tune, the 'chorus' cried out involuntarily to match arms hauling the rope with unsparing strength, if hummed by a comfortable sober face at ease, would no doubt look blatantly forced — but what lies in the breast of one working in the very middle of the ocean... a thing like that his wife, born in the capital and brought up only in the capital, once a delinquent girl, could not begin to imagine, not even in a dream.
notes: Em dashes kept only where Japanese has them. Rendered 不良少女あがり literally as 'once a delinquent girl' rather than softening; the evenness of the slight is part of the narration.

fork.question: Do they name the same thing in different words, or different things? They overlap on the unwritten-work/pond traffic, the snowscape detonation, the recurring slogans and the Nancy Lee pond scenes, but they are not the same crux restated: Option 0 makes the refusal to judge Taki the crux itself, while Option 1 makes judgement — title as indictment, comedy as verdict — and the three-register collision, including Taki's imitation of the workmen, separate cruxes. Choosing between them decides both the book's tone toward Taki and whether dialect/register is a load-bearing translation rule or a by-product of comic disproportion, and that choice will recur on every page; the text as quoted does not settle it, since the same scenes (p58–62, p160, p165–210) are cited by both sides for opposite tonal conclusions. Recommendation: proceed on Option 0 until the editor rules, because it contains Option 1's evidence without pre-deciding the verdict or a rigid concordance, whereas proceeding on Option 1 would bake a satirical stance and phrase-freezing into the draft that would be expensive to undo if the editor prefers the open reading.

options.author: first-read (Wonder)
options.case: - The gap between Taki's cherished, unwritten inner work and the squalid, absorbing business that actually fills his days — and the way the narration keeps lending the second the epic language of the first. Taki is a writer who has not really begun: he tells his wife the work is 'about half' done (p28) when in fact, once he took up his pen, he could write it 'in one burst' at any time — or so he believes; putting it into prose feels to him as clumsy and roundabout as making conversation. Everything grand in the story stays in his head, in quotation marks. Everything that actually happens is petty and physical: a pond dug for no good reason, carp that cannot be caught, a house about to be demolished and replaced by a warehouse, a telephone he suddenly decides to sell, carp suddenly worth four hundred yen, creditors at the door. The story's energy is the traffic between the two. His wife's casual remark that his finished seascape looks 'like a snowscape, in midsummer' (p58) detonates a paragraph of self-laceration in which all his realistic fiction and his whole foolish way of living become a botched 'snowscape', a blizzard rises, and he must flee across a white wilderness (p61–62). By section III the same man is bellowing orders at two workmen in a muddy pond like a general, then like an impresario inviting spectators up to the best seats, then discovering that this is more fun than any pleasure he knows (p165–179). In section IV the pumping-out of the pond, done by his assembled creditors, acquires 'the same underlying force as the chorus of Nancy Lee' (p210) — the sentimental whaling song he inherited from his father — while Taki himself is simply absent, gone to Tokyo 'to buy a lamp' (p212). If a translation resolves this into satire on a lazy writer, or into lyrical sympathy for a dreamer, it has chosen one pole and lost the story. For the English: Keep the comic disproportion intact. Do not make Taki's inner language beautiful and the pond business merely coarse background, and do not make the narration wink at him from outside. The same English must be able to inflate a carp-hunt into a battle, a chorus, a theatrical tableau, and then let it collapse into mud, cicadas and an unpaid bill. His quoted-back phrases — “the difficult work I'm holding in my head!”, “in one burst!”, “Nancy Lee”, “the telephone!”, “the terrifying blizzard!”, “nothing but a snowscape to look at!” — should recur recognisably, because in p160 the narration throws his own slogans back at him as they all scatter 'like goose down' while he sits glaring at the pond.
options.tradeoff: One crux, broadly framed: it preserves both poles and forbids a verdict, but gives no specific instruction on the workmen's vernacular or Taki's imitation of it.

options.author: crux-check (Wonder)
options.case:
- TAKI SEES THE WORLD IN REVERSE SEASON: HIS 'FINISHED' SUMMER SEASCAPE LOOKS — RIGHTLY — LIKE A SNOWSCAPE, BECAUSE HE LIVES IN AN UNWRITTEN, 'HELD-IN-THE-HEAD' FANTASY AND IS BLIND TO WHAT IS IN FRONT OF HIM. note.span: a fine dragon striking a pose across his whole back, with terrible wheeling clouds spreading their wings to the tips of both arms
note.body: A full-back dragon with clouds is a classic large tattoo design; a hannya is the horned demon-woman mask from No theatre, another traditional tattoo subject. The story shows one finished and one left as outline only.
note.author: notes

note.span: only the outline of a hannya mask traced, about eight-tenths finished, on the bare skin
note.body: Only the outline of the demon-mask is inked, about eight-tenths drawn, on bare skin. The text gives no reason for stopping.
note.author: notes

note.span: been meant perhaps for a Buddhist altar room
note.body: The guess is that the half-built extension was meant as a room holding the household Buddhist altar. Left unfinished for years, it has no electric light wired in.
note.author: notes

note.span: such things as "Ai Ai Ai" and "Valencia" and "Light Cavalry."
note.body: These were current popular tunes in late-1920s Japan, picked up from records, films and schoolboys and practised at home on the harmonica. The trailing (?) is in the Japanese.
note.author: notes

note.span: making the 'boat-song' Nancy Lee his refrain
note.body: Nancy Lee was an English-language sentimental song known in Japan as a sailors' song. Taki's father claims he learned it from sailors while shipping on an American whaler in his schooldays.
note.author: notes

note.body: Around four hundred yen is presented as a startlingly high sum, against the wife's ten yen in hand in the restaurant scene. The amount is what turns the nuisance carp into treasure.
note.author: notes

note.span: Put everything on the month-end bill
note.body: Putting things on the month-end bill means leaving shop and restaurant charges to be settled together at the end of the month. It was an ordinary way of running household accounts on credit.
note.author: notes

note.span: Shall we try a first throw with the cast net?
note.body: A cast net is a round weighted net thrown by hand over the water to fall over fish. A hand pump later borrowed from another villa is a portable pump worked by hand to drain the pond.
note.author: notes

payload.say: One part beginning at p1.

payload.why: This short story totals well under one reading limit and its four numbered sections form a single continuous arc, with the final section too brief to judge alone, so it is best held whole as one part.

payload.say: Reading (prose, crux first), open questions, and voice takes for Makino Shin'ichi's “Snowscape” (雪景色, 1927).

crux.for_the_english: Keep the comic disproportion intact. Do not make Taki's inner language beautiful and the pond business merely coarse background, and do not make the narration wink at him from outside. The same English must be able to inflate a carp-hunt into a battle, a chorus, a theatrical tableau, and then let it collapse into mud, cicadas and an unpaid bill. His quoted-back phrases — “the difficult work I'm holding in my head!”, “in one burst!”, “Nancy Lee”, “the telephone!”, “the terrifying blizzard!”, “nothing but a snowscape to look at!” — should recur recognisably, because in p160 the narration throws his own slogans back at him as they all scatter 'like goose down' while he sits glaring at the pond.
crux.point: The gap between Taki's cherished, unwritten inner work and the squalid, absorbing business that actually fills his days — and the way the narration keeps lending the second the epic language of the first.
crux.why: Taki is a writer who has not really begun: he tells his wife the work is 'about half' done (p28) when in fact, once he took up his pen, he could write it 'in one burst' at any time — or so he believes; putting it into prose feels to him as clumsy and roundabout as making conversation. Everything grand in the story stays in his head, in quotation marks. Everything that actually happens is petty and physical: a pond dug for no good reason, carp that cannot be caught, a house about to be demolished and replaced by a warehouse, a telephone he suddenly decides to sell, carp suddenly worth four hundred yen, creditors at the door. The story's energy is the traffic between the two. His wife's casual remark that his finished seascape looks 'like a snowscape, in midsummer' (p58) detonates a paragraph of self-laceration in which all his realistic fiction and his whole foolish way of living become a botched 'snowscape', a blizzard rises, and he must flee across a white wilderness (p61–62). By section III the same man is bellowing orders at two workmen in a muddy pond like a general, then like an impresario inviting spectators up to the best seats, then discovering that this is more fun than any pleasure he knows (p165–179). In section IV the pumping-out of the pond, done by his assembled creditors, acquires 'the same underlying force as the chorus of Nancy Lee' (p210) — the sentimental whaling song he inherited from his father — while Taki himself is simply absent, gone to Tokyo 'to buy a lamp' (p212). If a translation resolves this into satire on a lazy writer, or into lyrical sympathy for a dreamer, it has chosen one pole and lost the story.

payload.say: CONFIDENCE: HIGH ON BOTH. WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: EVIDENCE IN THE JAPANESE THAT THE REPEATED PHRASES I CALL DELIBERATE ECHOES ARE UNMARKED STOCK PHRASES WITH NO RETURN-VALUE IN p160 WOULD DEMOTE THE FIRST FROM A CRUX TO ORDINARY CONSISTENCY OF TERMINOLOGY.

FORK: The two readers substantially overlap but name different cruxes — Option 0's crux is the unresolved traffic between Taki's unwritten inner work and the petty business that borrows its epic language, with an express bar on resolving it into satire or sympathy; Option 1 adds a second, distinct crux in the collision of three registers and Taki's imitation of the workmen, hardens the snowscape/title into an indictment and a verdict, and imposes rigid concordance. I therefore do not pick: this is not one better than the other, it is a recurring question of tone and of whether register is itself load-bearing, and the scenes both cite (p58–62, p160, p165–210) support either tonal conclusion. I open a fork and recommend the run proceed on Option 0 in the meantime, since it preserves both poles and all the shared evidence without locking in the indictment or the concordance, which would be costly to reverse.

fork.question: Do they name the same thing in different words, or different things? They overlap on the unwritten-work/pond traffic, the snowscape detonation, the recurring slogans and the Nancy Lee pond scenes, but they are not the same crux restated: Option 0 makes the refusal to judge Taki the crux itself, while Option 1 makes judgement — title as indictment, comedy as verdict — and the three-register collision, including Taki's imitation of the workmen, separate cruxes.
